newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Far East Gold - IMF sales seen limited in effect.
newsitem.headline: Far East Gold - IMF sales seen limited in effect.

text.p: Asian gold dealers were eyeing the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) board meeting to discuss gold sales on Friday, but neither the IMF nor escalating Middle East tensions were likely to affect gold prices much, they said. One Hong Kong dealer said he doubted any decision would be reached by the IMF at all at its meeting in Washington.
"I don't think there'll even be a vote tonight," he said.

A handful of nations -- led by Germany -- have opposed the IMF's proposal to sell some five million ounces of its 104 million ounces of gold reserves over a period of time to bankroll debt relief for the world's poorest nations.

"If the Germans have more than 15 percent (of the vote), which they will, because the Austrians and the Finns will go with them, then they will never have a vote because it will look like dissent," the dealer said.
Germany feels IMF gold sales would establish a bad precedent, he noted.
"People will use the IMF news as an excuse to push prices down if they decide to sell that gold," one Singapore-based bank dealer said.
Another dealer said the mechanics of implementing such a sale would have to be worked out first and that would take time.
But he added: "The market's going to be marked down when this news comes out."
Most of the IMF gold would be offered to central banks around the world and if any of it reaches the market, the IMF would ensure it did so as unobtrusively as possible, dealers said.
Gold prices would remain range-bound and the prospect of another U.S. strike against Iraq would probably be ignored by the market unless the crisis escalated sharply, they added.

"They're probably going to bomb the Iraqis again, but it would have to escalate very badly for gold bullion to rally. No one really seems to care at this point," a trader in a European investment house said.
Spot gold was indicated at $382.40/90 an ounce in Hong Kong at midday on Friday, barely changed from its previous overnight close in New York.
With Asian physical demand and sentiment weak, spot gold is expected to languish in a range between $380 to $385 an ounce and the yellow metal may even test the $380 level, dealers said.
"Funds think the market is going to go lower, so we might see it go down to $380, although I think it will not break $380," a Singapore-based dealer said.
Singapore gold premiums over spot London prices were quoted at 35-45 U.S. cents an ounce against 35-55 cents last week after demand in the region softened, dealers said.
"Physical demand out here remained quiet, which is why premiums eased up a bit," one dealer said.
Hong Kong traders said a forecast by Union Bank of Switzerland analyst Andy Smith in London on Thursday, that spot gold could dive to $365 by the year end, was probably extreme.
Smith said a surge in speculative short positions on the New York Comex market, the fourth largest in 10 years, could foreshadow a short-covering rally followed by a price collapse.
With a contribution from Singapore
